title: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM, VARIANT TYPE
alt_titles: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM WITH NORMAL DNA REPAIR RATES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that xeroderma pigmentosum, variant type (XPV) is caused by mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (hRAD30), the human counterpart of yeast RAD30.

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum, variant type (XPV) is caused by mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (hRAD30).
checks.evidence_quote: We found that all XP-V cells examined carry mutations in their DNA polymerase eta gene.
checks.explanation: The paper finds mutations in all XP-V cells examined but concludes only tentatively that pol eta 'could be' the XPV gene product. The alias hRAD30 does not appear in the abstract.

checks.claim: The gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (hRAD30) is the human counterpart of yeast RAD30.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we show that this polymerase is a human homologue of the yeast Rad30 protein, recently identified as DNA polymerase eta.
checks.explanation: The abstract identifies the polymerase as the human homologue of yeast Rad30.

paragraphs.text: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder with an increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers (Masutani et al., 1999). XPV patients show the clinical features of xeroderma pigmentosum, including more skin cancer. However, their cells have a normal or nearly normal rate of nucleotide excision repair and are only slightly more sensitive than normal cells to UV cytotoxicity, although they are significantly more sensitive to the mutagenic effect of UV (Wang et al., 1991). Unlike cells from XP groups A to G, XP-V cells carry out normal nucleotide excision repair but are defective in replicating UV-damaged DNA (Lehmann et al., 1975; Masutani et al., 1999).

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder which is associated with increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) involves an increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.
checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder which is associated with increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.

checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) variant patients show the clinical characteristics of the disease, with increased frequencies of skin cancer

checks.claim: XPV cells have a normal or nearly normal rate of nucleotide excision repair.
checks.evidence_quote: their cells have a normal, or nearly normal, rate of nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced DNA damage

checks.claim: XPV cells are only slightly more sensitive than normal cells to UV cytotoxicity.
checks.evidence_quote: are only slightly more sensitive than normal cells to the cytotoxic effect of UV radiation

checks.evidence_quote: However, they are significantly more sensitive to its mutagenic effect.

checks.evidence_quote: XP-V cells carry out normal nucleotide-excision repair processes but are defective in their replication of ultraviolet-damaged DNA.

paragraphs.text: Cleaver et al. (1980) found that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture could not be distinguished from the XP variant in UV-induced unscheduled DNA synthesis, strand breakage during repair, chain growth during semiconservative replication with or without caffeine, or recovery of replication. They concluded that the term 'pigmented xerodermoid' was redundant.

checks.claim: Cleaver et al. (1980) found that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture could not be distinguished from the XP variant in UV-induced unscheduled DNA synthesis.
checks.evidence_quote: XP and pigmented xerodermoid cell cultures were irradiated with ultraviolet light and unscheduled DNA synthesis, strand breakage during repair, chain growth during semiconservative DNA replication with or without caffeine, and the recovery of DNA replication were determined. It is concluded that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture is indistinguishable from the XP variant
checks.explanation: The abstract lists unscheduled DNA synthesis among the assays and concludes that the two culture types are indistinguishable. It does not give results for each assay separately.

It is concluded that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture is indistinguishable from the XP variant
checks.explanation: The abstract lists strand breakage during repair among the assays, and the overall conclusion is that the cultures are indistinguishable.

checks.evidence_quote: It is concluded that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture is indistinguishable from the XP variant and the former term is therefore redundant.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this conclusion directly.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (2000) studied 2 independent families that included 2 photosensitive patients identified as having xeroderma pigmentosum variant. One family was Japanese. In the patients' cells, recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation was reduced.

checks.evidence_quote: In this study we assess the cellular markers in two independent families that included two photosensitive patients that were identified as xeroderma pigmentosum variant.

checks.claim: One of the 2 xeroderma pigmentosum variant families studied by Itoh et al. (2000) was Japanese.
checks.evidence_quote: Each of these mutations were absent in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.
checks.explanation: The abstract never says the family is Japanese. This is only implied by the Japanese control population.

checks.claim: In cells from the xeroderma pigmentosum variant patients studied by Itoh et al. (2000), recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation was reduced.
checks.evidence_quote: only xeroderma pigmentosum variant cells exhibited normal unscheduled DNA synthesis, normal recovery of RNA synthesis, but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis (51 +/- 6% the rate relative to normal controls)
checks.explanation: The reduced recovery is described for XPV cells in general (from the earlier report). The abstract does not give results for these two patients' cells specifically.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (1996) found that caffeine enhanced the reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation in XPV cells.

checks.evidence_quote: This reduction of DNA synthesis is enhanced in the presence of caffeine.
checks.explanation: The paper says caffeine makes the reduction in DNA synthesis worse, so recovery is further impaired. The draft says caffeine 'enhanced the reduced recovery', which could be read as caffeine improving recovery. The gist is right but the wording is ambiguous.

paragraphs.text: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Johnson et al. (1999) identified nonsense or frameshift mutations in hRAD30 in XP variant cell lines. In a family reported by Itoh et al. (2000), the affected individual inherited 2 heterozygous missense mutations from heterozygous parents. The parents were not affected.

checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by a high incidence of skin cancers.
checks.explanation: Abstract states XP generally is autosomal recessive, not specifically the variant form.

checks.claim: Johnson et al. (1999) identified nonsense or frameshift mutations in hRAD30 in XP variant cell lines.

checks.claim: In a xeroderma pigmentosum variant family reported by Itoh et al. (2000), the affected individual inherited 2 heterozygous missense mutations from heterozygous parents.
checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms inheritance of 2 heterozygous missense mutations, and elsewhere describes the parents as heterozygotic.

checks.claim: The heterozygous parents of the xeroderma pigmentosum variant patient reported by Itoh et al. (2000) were not affected.

checks.explanation: The parents' cells are mostly normal and only the patients are called photosensitive. However, the abstract never explicitly says the parents are clinically unaffected.

paragraphs.text: Fujiwara et al. (1981) studied an 8-year-old boy (UV81KO) who had acute recurrent sunburns and no physical or neuromental retardation. His skin showed lowered minimal erythema doses between 280 and 300 nm. His fibroblasts were 5-fold more sensitive than normal cells to killing by 254-nm UV and had a higher baseline level of sister chromatid exchanges (10-12 per cell vs 5 per cell in normal cells). The cells showed no detectable defect in nucleotide excision repair or in replicative bypass. However, they failed to recover DNA synthesis after UV irradiation at doses at which normal cells recovered. Fujiwara et al. (1981) concluded that these features set the patient clearly apart from xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, the 11961 disorder, and Bloom syndrome. They proposed that he had a new photodermatosis with a defect in the recovery of DNA synthesis after UV exposure.

paragraphs.text: Using a cell-free trans-lesion synthesis assay, Masutani et al. (1999) isolated a DNA polymerase from HeLa cells that bypassed UV-induced thymine dimers in XP-V cell extracts. They identified it as a human homolog of yeast Rad30 (DNA polymerase eta), a member of the UmuC/DinB/Rev1 family of damage-bypass replication proteins. All XP-V cells they examined carried mutations in the DNA polymerase eta gene. Recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrected the inability of XP-V cell extracts to replicate DNA past thymine dimers. The authors concluded that DNA polymerase eta could be the XPV gene product.

checks.evidence_quote: Using an improved cell-free assay for trans-lesion DNA synthesis, we have recently isolated a DNA polymerase from HeLa cells that continues replication on damaged DNA by bypassing ultraviolet-induced thymine dimers in XP-V cell extracts.

checks.claim: Masutani et al. (1999) identified the thymine dimer-bypassing polymerase as a human homolog of yeast Rad30 (DNA polymerase eta).
checks.evidence_quote: Here we show that this polymerase is a human homologue of the yeast Rad30 protein, recently identified as DNA polymerase eta.

checks.claim: DNA polymerase eta is a member of the UmuC/DinB/Rev1 family of damage-bypass replication proteins.
checks.evidence_quote: This polymerase and yeast Rad30 are members of a family of damage-bypass replication proteins which comprises the Escherichia coli proteins UmuC and DinB and the yeast Rev1 protein.

checks.claim: All XP-V cells examined by Masutani et al. (1999) carried mutations in the DNA polymerase eta gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We found that all XP-V cells examined carry mutations in their DNA polymerase eta gene.

checks.claim: Recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrected the inability of XP-V cell extracts to replicate DNA past thymine dimers.
checks.evidence_quote: Recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrects the inability of XP-V cell extracts to carry out DNA replication by bypassing thymine dimers on damaged DNA.

checks.claim: Masutani et al. (1999) concluded that DNA polymerase eta could be the XPV gene product.
checks.evidence_quote: Together, these results indicate that DNA polymerase eta could be the XPV gene product.

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese XPV family, Itoh et al. (2000) confirmed that the patient had inherited 2 heterozygous missense mutations from heterozygous parents. One was an A-to-G transition at nucleotide 1840 resulting in a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution. The other was an A-to-C transversion at nucleotide 2003 affecting lys589 (K589). Neither mutation was found in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.

checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not name the gene (DNA polymerase eta) and does not explicitly say the family is Japanese.

checks.evidence_quote: Each of these mutations were absent in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.

paragraphs.text: Lehmann et al. (1975) found that XP variant cells, which have normal excision repair, synthesized DNA abnormally after UV irradiation. Newly synthesized low-molecular-weight DNA took much longer than in normal cells to be converted to high-molecular-weight DNA. Caffeine strongly inhibited this slow conversion in XP variant cells but had no effect in normal cells. Two cell lines from excision-defective classes of xeroderma pigmentosum showed intermediate results: both the time needed to convert newly synthesized DNA to high molecular weight and the caffeine inhibition of this process fell between those of normal and XP variant cells.

checks.claim: Lehmann et al. (1975) found that XP variant cells have normal excision repair.
checks.evidence_quote: There is, however, one class of these patients whose cells are completely normal in this excision repair process.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that cells from this class have completely normal excision repair.

checks.claim: Lehmann et al. (1975) found that XP variant cells synthesized DNA abnormally after UV irradiation.
checks.evidence_quote: We have found that these cells have an abnormality in the manner in which DNA is synthesized after UV-irradiation.

checks.claim: In XP variant cells, newly synthesized low-molecular-weight DNA took much longer than in normal cells to be converted to high-molecular-weight DNA after UV irradiation.
checks.evidence_quote: The time taken to convert initially low-molecular-weight DNA synthesized in UV-irradiated cells into high-molecular-weight DNA similar in size to that in untreated cells is much greater in these variants than in normal cells.

checks.claim: Caffeine strongly inhibited the slow conversion of low- to high-molecular-weight DNA in XP variant cells.
checks.evidence_quote: Furthermore, this slow conversion of low to high-molecular-weight newly synthesized DNA is drastically inhibited by caffeine, which has no effect in normal cells.
checks.explanation: The abstract says caffeine 'drastically' inhibits the slow conversion, which matches 'strongly inhibited'.

checks.evidence_quote: Two cell lines from classes of xeroderma pigmentosum that are defective in excision-repair show intermediate effects, with regard to both the time taken to convert newly synthesized DNA to high molecular weight

paragraphs.text: Cleaver et al. (1980) proposed that XP variant cells lack a gene product that lets normal cells replicate DNA without interruption at UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. As a result, replication forks were blocked more often and at lower doses. They suggested that the link between this defect and the high rate of actinic carcinogenesis pointed to an important role for disturbed DNA replication in human carcinogenesis.

checks.evidence_quote: The defect common to these cell types appears to be the loss of a gene product that permits normal cells to replicate DNA without interruption at damaged sites (u.v.-induced pyrimidine dimers).

checks.claim: Cleaver et al. (1980) proposed that in XP variant cells, replication forks were blocked more often and at lower UV doses.
checks.evidence_quote: The consequence of this loss is that replication forks are blocked more frequently and at lower doses in XP variant cells.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly. It says only "lower doses", but the cells were UV-irradiated, so these are UV doses.

checks.claim: Cleaver et al. (1980) suggested that the link between the XP variant replication defect and the high rate of actinic carcinogenesis pointed to an important role for disturbed DNA replication in human carcinogenesis.
checks.evidence_quote: The correlation between this defect and high levels of actinic carcinogenesis in these patients points to an important role for perturbations in DNA replication in human carcinogenesis.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1991) transfected an XP variant cell line with a UV-irradiated shuttle vector carrying the supF gene as a mutation target. Mutant frequency rose linearly with dose, with a slope 5 times steeper than in normal cells. Of 53 independent mutants, 52 had base substitutions, and 62 of the 64 substitutions involved a dipyrimidine. In XP variant cells, 28% of the mutations involved A.T base pairs, compared with 11% in normal cells. Most of these were at position 136, the middle of a run of 3 A.T base pairs. Assuming the excision rate is the same in both cell lines, the authors suggested that XP variant cells are less likely than normal cells to incorporate dAMP opposite photoproduct bases. They proposed that this could account for the UV hypermutability of XP variant cells.

checks.evidence_quote: we transfected an XP variant cell line with a UV-irradiated (at 254 nm) shuttle vector carrying the supF gene as a target for mutations

checks.claim: In XP variant cells transfected with UV-irradiated supF shuttle vector, mutant frequency rose linearly with UV dose.
checks.evidence_quote: The frequency of mutants increased linearly with dose

checks.claim: The slope of the UV dose-response for supF mutant frequency was 5 times steeper in XP variant cells than in normal cells.
checks.evidence_quote: The frequency of mutants increased linearly with dose, but with a slope 5 times steeper than that seen with normal cells.

checks.claim: Of 53 independent supF mutants from XP variant cells, 52 had base substitutions.
checks.evidence_quote: 52 of 53 independent mutants generated in the XP variant cells contained base substitutions

checks.evidence_quote: with 62 of 64 of the substitutions involving a dipyrimidine

checks.evidence_quote: Twenty-eight percent of the mutations involved A.T base pairs, with the majority found at position 136, the middle of a run of three A.T base pairs. (In the normal cells, this value was only 11%.)

checks.evidence_quote: with the majority found at position 136, the middle of a run of three A.T base pairs

paragraphs.text: Using DNA combing, Despras et al. (2010) showed that after UV irradiation, the translesion synthesis defect in XP-V cells led to a strong reduction in active replication forks and a high proportion of stalled forks. Low UVC doses caused extensive single-strand DNA formation and over-activation of the ATR/Chk1 pathway. Low-dose caffeine given after irradiation decreased Chk1 activation and abolished DNA synthesis in XP-V cells. Chk1 inhibition by UCN-01 increased fork stalling and, like caffeine, sensitized XP-V cells to UVC. The authors concluded that in the absence of pol-eta, Chk1 becomes essential for resuming replication through fork stabilization, which explains the caffeine sensitivity of XP-V cells.

checks.claim: Using DNA combing, Despras et al. (2010) showed that after UV irradiation, the translesion synthesis defect in XP-V cells led to a strong reduction in active replication forks.
checks.evidence_quote: Using DNA combing, we showed that translesion synthesis defect leads to a strong reduction in the number of active replication forks and a high proportion of stalled forks in human cells
checks.explanation: The abstract states this result. The UV-irradiation context is implied by the study design.

checks.claim: Despras et al. (2010) showed that after UV irradiation, XP-V cells had a high proportion of stalled replication forks.
checks.evidence_quote: translesion synthesis defect leads to a strong reduction in the number of active replication forks and a high proportion of stalled forks in human cells
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a high proportion of stalled forks.

checks.claim: In XP-V cells, low UVC doses caused extensive single-strand DNA formation.
checks.evidence_quote: extensive regions of single-strand DNA are formed during replication in irradiated XP-V cells, leading to an over-activation of ATR/Chk1 pathway after low UVC doses
checks.explanation: The abstract states that extensive single-strand DNA forms in irradiated XP-V cells at low UVC doses.

checks.claim: In XP-V cells, low UVC doses caused over-activation of the ATR/Chk1 pathway.
checks.evidence_quote: leading to an over-activation of ATR/Chk1 pathway after low UVC doses

checks.claim: Low-dose caffeine given after irradiation decreased Chk1 activation in XP-V cells.
checks.evidence_quote: Addition of a low concentration of caffeine post-irradiation, although inefficient to restore S-phase progression, significantly decreases Chk1 activation and abrogates DNA synthesis in XP-V cells.

checks.claim: Low-dose caffeine given after irradiation abolished DNA synthesis in XP-V cells.
checks.evidence_quote: Addition of a low concentration of caffeine post-irradiation, although inefficient to restore S-phase progression, significantly decreases Chk1 activation and abrogates DNA synthesis in XP-V cells.
checks.explanation: The paper's 'abrogates' means the same as the draft's 'abolished'.

checks.claim: Chk1 inhibition by UCN-01 increased replication fork stalling in XP-V cells.
checks.evidence_quote: it aggravates replication defect in XP-V cells by increasing fork stalling
checks.explanation: The abstract says UCN-01 increases fork stalling in XP-V cells.

checks.claim: Chk1 inhibition by UCN-01, like caffeine, sensitized XP-V cells to UVC.

checks.evidence_quote: In the absence of poleta, Chk1 kinase becomes essential for replication resumption by alternative pathways, via fork stabilization.

checks.explanation: The abstract presents caffeine sensitivity as the question being studied and implies that the Chk1 dependence answers it. However, the stated conclusion never explicitly says the Chk1 role explains the caffeine sensitivity, so the draft goes slightly beyond the text.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (1996) described a simple autoradiographic method for diagnosing XP variant. It measures 3 DNA repair markers in patient fibroblasts and compares them with adjacent normal cells on the same coverslips: unscheduled DNA synthesis (UDS), recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation. Among the hereditary photosensitive disorders tested (XP, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome), only XPV cells showed normal UDS and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis, at about 50% of control. Because each photosensitive disorder gave a different combination of the 3 markers, the authors proposed that the method also offers a systematic basis for diagnosing these diseases.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (2000) found that recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV in XPV cells was 51% of normal and fell further to 36% in the presence of nontoxic caffeine. Cells from heterozygous parents of XPV patients had normal UDS, normal recovery of RNA synthesis, and normal recovery of replicative DNA synthesis. However, with 1 mM caffeine, their recovery of replicative DNA synthesis was reduced (53% of normal) and their UV survival was slightly reduced. The authors suggested that XPV heterozygotes can be identified by UV sensitivity in the presence of nontoxic caffeine.

paragraphs.text: Masutani et al. (1999) found mutations in the DNA polymerase eta gene in all XP-V cells they examined. The individual mutations and their zygosity were not specified. Recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrected the inability of XP-V cell extracts to replicate DNA past thymine dimers.

checks.evidence_quote: Recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrects the inability of XP-V cell extracts to carry out DNA replication by bypassing thymine dimers on damaged DNA.

paragraphs.text: Johnson et al. (1999) identified nonsense or frameshift mutations in hRAD30 in XP variant cell lines. Of the 8 mutations identified, 7 were predicted to result in a severely truncated hRad30 protein.

paragraphs.text: In a photosensitive Japanese patient with XPV, Itoh et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous A-to-G transition at nucleotide 1840 resulting in a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution. The patient had inherited it, together with a second missense mutation (2003A-C), from heterozygous parents. The mutation was not found in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals. The patient's cells showed reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation.
